title: Explainable Quantum Deep Learning Framework Integrating Vision Transformers and Federated Intelligence for Smart Healthcare Applications
abstract: Modern healthcare systems increasingly rely on artificial intelligence, deep learning, and medical imaging technologies for accurate disease diagnosis and clinical decision-making. However, conventional AI systems still face challenges related to interpretability, computational complexity, centralized data dependency, and patient privacy. This paper presents an Explainable Quantum Deep Learning Framework integrating Vision Transformers, Federated Intelligence, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for smart healthcare applications. The proposed framework combines quantum-inspired optimization, multimodal medical data analysis, transformer-based feature extraction, and decentralized federated learning to improve diagnostic accuracy, scalability, privacy preservation, and interpretability. Explainability mechanisms including SHAP and Grad-CAM are incorporated to enhance physician trust and clinical transparency. Experimental evaluation demonstrates superior performance in biomedical image classification and disease prediction compared with conventional deep learning models, providing a scalable solution for next-generation intelligent healthcare systems.

title: 五维原生模型:内生约束神经网络架构与AI范式转换
abstract: 存在即五维。AI问世前,自然与社会为人类文明设定了相对稳定的边界与方向,结构维只需组织数据,储备与强度自然可控。AI以Transformer单一结构维范式打破了五维平衡:边界被无限放大、方向摇摆不定、储备断裂、强度失控。西方“大力出奇迹”的参数膨胀路线试图以结构扩张隐式覆盖其余四维,必然导致系统性危机。本文提出五维原生模型(5D-NM),以五维数学为桥梁,将五维系统论从哲学存在论直接下沉为神经网络元架构,通过五维嵌入、五维注意力与五维协同损失,使边界警觉、结构生成、储备溯源、方向校准与强度调节内生于同一参数空间,κ直接参与梯度下降,实现端到端的可训练、可度量、可演化。

title: Does Prompt Quality Actually Matter More Than Prompt Quantity? An Empirical Study on
abstract: Few-shot prompting is a widely used technique in which input-output examples guide a large language model toward a desired output. This study investigates whether the quality of few-shot examples has a greater impact on LLM output accuracy than quantity. Through a controlled 3×4×5 factorial experiment (600 LLM calls to GPT-4o-mini), we demonstrate that 3 high-quality examples outperform 10 low-quality examples by 22.7 percentage points. High-quality prompts achieved 86.4% mean accuracy vs. 65.2% for low-quality prompts. The effect was most pronounced in JSON extraction (+65.8 pp). These findings advise practitioners to prioritize example curation over accumulation when designing few-shotprompts for production AI systems.

title: Sequence Modeling Architectures: Foundations [Special Issue on the Mathematics of Deep Learning]
abstract: With the success of deep learning in the past decade, neural networks transitioned from simple layer stacking to sophisticated, highly complex designs. This article provides an overview of such deep learning architectures for sequence modeling, with a focus on their core mathematical principles: 1) we review the evolution of common sequence models from recurrent neural networks (RNNs), to Transformers, and modern state-space models (SSMs), exploring their foundational components such as gating, attention, and linear dynamical systems mechanisms. 2) We present general linear sequence mixers as a unifying framework to highlight the relationship between architectures and compare them in terms of inductive biases and algorithmic complexity. 3) We examine how practical considerations such as parallelizability and hardware awareness dictate their success. Finally, we discuss their impact on diverse fields of signal processing, including time-series analysis, natural language, and computer vision.

title: A17-05 Comparing Cross-Site Validation, Transfer Learning, and Independent Training for ICU Mortality Prediction: A U.S. Multicenter Study
abstract: Abstract Rationale Deploying machine learning models across health systems remains challenging, with widely implemented algorithms such as commercial sepsis prediction demonstrating poor external validity. While intensive care unit (ICU) mortality prediction models can support clinical decision-making, optimal strategies for model transfer remain unclear. We evaluated three deployment strategies across hospitals to offer practical, evidence-based guidance for implementing prediction models in the ICU. Methods We conducted a federated analysis using the Common Longitudinal ICU data Format (CLIF) Consortium, a geographically diverse network of 9 academic health systems. We identified adult patients admitted to ICUs at 9 sites between 2018-2024 (2018-2023 for training and validation, 2024 for testing) who survived for at least 24 hours. Patient demographics, vital signs, laboratory results, and respiratory support data (52 variables) were extracted from electronic health records (EHR) 24 hours after ICU admission. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality occurring at any time following the initial 24-hour period. We trained gradient boosted machine (XGBoost) and neural network binary classifiers to predict in-hospital mortality using three deployment strategies: 1) Cross-Site Validation, wherein a model trained at a single source institution was tested on all other sites as is; 2) Transfer Learning, wherein the source model was fine-tuned with a limited subset of local site data; and 3) Independent Training, wherein models were trained exclusively on target site data without leveraging prior knowledge. We evaluated discrimination using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration metrics, and decision curve analysis, following TRIPOD-AI guidelines. Results The overall cohort comprised 428,924 ICU hospital encounters (mean age 61 years, 45% female). Overall mortality was 9% (range 7-13% across sites). For XGBoost models, the cross-site validation AUC was 0.85 [95% CI 0.84-0.87], transfer learning AUC 0.86 [95% CI 0.84-0.87], and independent training AUC 0.87 [95% CI 0.85-0.89]. For neural networks, cross-site validation AUC was 0.81 [95% CI 0.75-0.87], transfer learning AUC 0.86 [95% CI 0.82-0.90], and independent training AUC 0.86 [95% CI 0.82-0.90]. Brier scores ranged from 0.05 to 0.13, improving with transfer learning and independent training (Figure 1). Conclusions Across nine health systems, transfer learning for neural networks matched independent training performance while XGBoost demonstrated consistent discrimination and calibration across all approaches. Based on these findings, optimal deployment strategies may differ by modeling technique. However, local validation in a specific patient population is essential, regardless of deployment approach. Future research should evaluate these patterns across other modeling techniques and ICU outcomes. This abstract is funded by: Institute for Translational Medicine Pilot Award

title: Repurposing Image Diffusion Models for Adversarial Synthetic Structured Data: A Case Study of Ground Truth Drift
abstract: Public image diffusion models are now powerful enough that an attacker without the resources to train a tabular-specific generator may repurpose one off the shelf. This study tests that possibility directly. An unmodified Stable Diffusion U-Net is applied to the UCI Adult Income dataset by reshaping each row into a small single-channel pseudo-image. The architecture's inductive bias toward spatial locality makes feature placement a design variable, and several layouts are tested. However, this is only the beginning of the story, as this paper also draws two philosophical distinctions. One separates statistical from perceptual realism: whether synthetic content holds up to a machine's correlation audits or a human's sensory inspection. The other introduces synthetic evidence as a category alongside synthetic media: AI-generated material whose consumer is a machine in a closed evidentiary pipeline rather than a person in an open information system. An attacker succeeds with synthetic evidence by thinking like the machine that will receive it. And the more the attacker succeeds, the more they can induce ground truth drift: the silent reclassification of AI-generated outputs as authentic when reused in pipelines that do not interrogate their provenance.

title: Learning Multimodal Energy-Based Model with Multimodal Variational Auto-Encoder via MCMC Revision
abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) are a flexible class of deep generative models and are well-suited to capture complex dependencies in multimodal data. However, learning multimodal EBM by maximum likelihood requires Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling in the joint data space, where noise-initialized Langevin dynamics often mixes poorly and fails to discover coherent inter-modal relationships. Multimodal VAEs have made progress in capturing such inter-modal dependencies by introducing a shared latent generator and a joint inference model. However, both the shared latent generator and joint inference model are parameterized as unimodal Gaussian (or Laplace), which severely limits their ability to approximate the complex structure induced by multimodal data. In this work, we study the learning problem of the multimodal EBM, shared latent generator, and joint inference model. We present a learning framework that effectively interweaves their MLE updates with corresponding MCMC refinements in both the data and latent spaces. Specifically, the generator is learned to produce coherent multimodal samples that serve as strong initial states for EBM sampling, while the inference model is learned to provide informative latent initializations for generator posterior sampling. Together, these two models serve as complementary models that enable effective EBM sampling and learning, yielding realistic and coherent multimodal EBM samples. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior performance for multimodal synthesis quality and coherence compared to various baselines. We conduct various analyses and ablation studies to validate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed multimodal framework.

title: Thinking in Text and Images: Interleaved Vision--Language Reasoning Traces for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires plans that are both logically coherent and geometrically grounded. Existing Vision-Language-Action policies usually hide planning in latent states or expose only one modality: text-only chain-of-thought encodes causal order but misses spatial constraints, while visual prediction provides geometric cues but often remains local and semantically underconstrained. We introduce Interleaved Vision--Language Reasoning (IVLR), a policy framework built around \trace{}, an explicit intermediate representation that alternates textual subgoals with visual keyframes over the full task horizon. At test time, a single native multimodal transformer self-generates this global semantic-geometric trace from the initial observation and instruction, caches it, and conditions a closed-loop action decoder on the trace, original instruction, and current observation. Because standard robot datasets lack such traces, we construct pseudo-supervision by temporally segmenting demonstrations and captioning each stage with a vision-language model. Across simulated benchmarks for long-horizon manipulation and visual distribution shift, \method{} reaches 95.5\% average success on LIBERO, including 92.4\% on LIBERO-Long, and 59.4\% overall success on SimplerEnv-WidowX. Ablations show that both modalities are necessary: without traces, LIBERO-Long success drops to 37.7\%; text-only and vision-only traces reach 62.0\% and 68.4\%, while the full interleaved trace reaches 92.4\%. Stress tests with execution perturbations and masked trace content show moderate degradation, suggesting that the trace can tolerate local corruption and moderate execution drift, but remains limited under stale or incorrect global plans.

title: A Comparative Study of Machine Learning Methods for Credit Card Fraud Detection
abstract: The problem of credit card fraud causes significant financial losses to businesses and consumers and prompts studies on effective ways of detecting fraud. Here we examine a publicly available dataset of credit card transactions (a total of 10,000) (151 fraudulent, 9,849 legitimate) and create supervised learning models to categorize credit card transactions. We train classifiers of logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost, and the class imbalance will be addressed through the use of class-weighting. Performance is also assessed using accuracy, recall, F1-score, and ROC AUC (Receiver Operating Characteristics Area under the Curve) as sole accuracy will not suffice in the unbalanced data scenario. Evidence indicates that logistic regression achieves high recall (91 ) but low precision (23%), which is a high number of false alarm. Compared to the above, random forest is balanced (precision 100, recall 58, F1 =0.73), and the XGBoost is almost perfect in discrimination (precision 100, recall 97.8, F1 =0.99, ROC AUC =0.999). The results are consistent with available literature, which indicates that ensemble techniques (random forests and boosting) are more effective than simple models in detecting fraud. We speculate about the implications of this trade-off on a real-world deployment, as well as providing future work directions.

title: FROM AUTOMATION TO AUTONOMY: THE STRATEGIC ROLE OF GENERATIVE AND AGENTIC AI IN BANKING
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping the banking sector, enabling a transition from traditional rulebased automation toward more intelligent and autonomous systems.In particular, the emergence of generative and agentic AI represents a significant shift in how banks design services, make decisions, and deliver customer value.While prior title: Pop Lyrics through Time: Challenges in Corpus-Based Modeling of Linguistic and Emotional Dynamics in German Pop Lyrics
abstract: This paper presents a large-scale diachronic analysis of German pop lyrics based on a linguistically rich, TEIencoded monitoring corpus.We describe multi-layer annotation and reproducible workflows for deriving higherlevel features at scale, including lexical diversity indices, a pronoun-based subjectivity measure, modal particle density, and a length-normalized sentiment intensity score.Particular attention is paid to the development and evaluation of pipelines for two notoriously challenging phenomena: modal particles and sentiment.For modal particles, we build a manually curated gold standard and train sequence models whose performance we relate to inter-annotator agreement.For sentiment, we integrate a lexicon-based resource with a dedicated human annotation experiment to assess reliability and alignment with expert judgments.On this basis, we investigate how structural and affective features co-vary in the corpus and how they change over time, showing, among other trends, declining lexical diversity and sentiment intensity alongside a slight increase in first-and second-person pronouns.Beyond the empirical findings, the paper highlights practical challenges in managing culturally specific corpora, and makes evaluation materials available to support transparent, reusable corpus-based research on popular music and related domains.

title: Subevent Structure as a Predictor of Entity Identity Change in Procedural Text
abstract: We test whether the subevent structure encoded in VerbNet-GL predicts entity identity change in procedural text, using only the verb's lexical specification and no training data.From each VN verb class's SEMANTICS block we extract an aspectual classification and an I/O count, yielding a predicted dynamic event topology (DET).On the observation side, ten large language models (LLMs) annotate per-entity dynamic object mode (DOM) labels over ∼3100 OpenPI steps, from which we derive observed DET for comparison.The VN-only predictor achieves 67.4% precision (F1 = 0.35) for transformation, showing that formal subevent structure carries genuine predictive signal only for the most common topology, but low performance for other topologies.For events VN predicts as having no result state, only 24% are confirmed as no-change by silver, indicating that the remaining outcomes arise from the argument side of the composition.These results provide empirical evidence that event semantics is distributed across predicate and argument: the VN supplies the subeventual skeleton, but is not sufficient to determine the final outcome.

title: Speaker Normalization via Voice Conversion Reveals a Human-Machine Dissociation in Dialect Classification
abstract: This study evaluates whether Retrieval-based Voice Conversion (RVC) can be used to normalize speaker-specific variability while preserving dialect-relevant acoustic cues, and what the response of human and machine systems to this manipulation reveals about the architecture of dialect recognition.In two perception experiments, speech samples from nine German dialect regions were presented either in their original form or after conversion to a single target speaker.We compared overall accuracy, confusion structures, item-level response distributions, and the interaction between listener origin and target dialect across conditions.Human classification remained stable under voice conversion.Accuracy did not differ between conditions, confusion matrices were highly correlated, and item-level divergences were minimal.The interaction between listener origin and target dialect-reflecting systematic regional bias-remained invariant.These findings indicate that RVC does not distort perceptually relevant dialectal cues and that human dialect recognition is robust to speaker normalization.In contrast, we evaluated a deep learning model under matched conditions: model accuracy improved significantly under RVC, while human performance remained unchanged.This dissociation reframes RVC as an experimental probe for investigating the divergence between human and machine speech processing, suggesting that this divergence is rooted in fundamentally different representational architectures.

title: Unigoa@CHiPSAL 2026: Early vs Late Fusion for Multimodal Hate and Sentiment Detection in Nepali Memes
abstract: Internet memes pose significant challenges for automatic content moderation due to the interaction of visual and textual cues, sarcasm, and cultural context.In this work, we participate in the CHiPSAL 2026 shared task on multimodal hate and sentiment understanding in Nepali memes.The task consists of two subtasks: binary hate speech detection and three-class sentiment classification.We investigate both early-fusion and late-fusion multimodal architectures.Our primary system employs a late-fusion dual-encoder architecture combining XLM-RoBERTa for multilingual text representation and CLIP for visual encoding.We further evaluate an early-fusion ViLT-based joint vision-language transformer using NepBERTa tokenization as a baseline.Experimental results show that late-fusion models consistently outperform early-fusion architectures, particularly for code-mixed memes containing Devanagari Nepali and Roman-script English text.Our best system achieves a Macro-F1 of 0.6564 for hate speech detection and 0.4859 for sentiment classification.We provide analysis highlighting the challenges of multilingual code-mixing, sarcasm, and implicit sentiment in low-resource multimodal settings.

title: A Generative AI-Enabled Framework for Reproducible Feature Selection and Knowledge Extraction
abstract: Feature selection is a critical stage in machine learning pipelines, yet the process is often complex and loosely structured. It typically involves multiple iterative steps, such as data pre-processing, relevance determination, and model-based evaluation, that are rarely captured by consistent metadata or transparent decision criteria. As a result, effective feature selection frequently depends on substantial domain expertise and is commonly performed and validated through manual, ad hoc procedures. To address these challenges, we present a metadata-driven agentic system for explainable and reproducible feature selection. The system integrates structured metadata, transparent audit trails, and a generative AI agent for analysis, reporting, and knowledge extraction.

title: A Constraint-Native Execution Fabric for Adaptive Control of Autonomous Systems
abstract: introduction: BlueGate A Constraint-Native Execution Fabric for Adaptive Control of Autonomous Systems The BlueGate Constrained Execution Fabric represents a fully synthetic, constraint native architecture designed to govern autonomous action through a unified substrate of fourteencoupled evaluation primitives, projection based optimization, adaptive parameter tuning, and cryptographic audit chaining. At its core, the system functions as a hybrid control mechanism that seamlessly integrates constrained quadratic programming for resource and semantic projection, probabilistic risk assessment through trust drift monitoring and Byzantine scoring, policy enforcement via role based authority and lineage validation, dynamic graph topology tracking, an online learning loop that continuously adjusts constraint sensitivity, and an immutable hash chained execution log that guarantees forensic verifiability. The architecture is deliberately engineered to eliminate the binary rigidity of traditional rule engines by distinguishing between hard constraints that trigger immediate state rollback and rejection, and soft constraints that route actions through a sequential least squares programming optimizer to find the minimally altered, feasible representation of the original intent. The fourteen primitives span six functional domains and operate in parallel during every evaluation cycle. The execution integrity domain enforces causal ordering to ensure that no action references future or unestablished causal counters, maintains state consistency by bounding deviations from a consensus estimate within a strict epsilon threshold, and validates temporal validity by rejecting any action whose expiration timestamp has been surpassed by the deterministic simulation clock. The resource constraints domain governs the system envelope by hard limiting energy, compute, bandwidth, and thermal metrics against predefined maximums, while simultaneously evaluating state transition feasibility through a linear dynamics model that compares predicted state evolution against actual outcomes to detect modeling divergence. The trust system domain continuously monitors network health through three complementary mechanisms that track the norm of trust vector drift against a row stochastic diffusion baseline, compute the Kullback-Leibler divergence between current and estimated belief distributions, and calculate a Byzantine score that flags nodes whose trust values statistically deviate from their immediate neighbors, with isolated nodes defaulting to a midpoint baseline to prevent false positives. The authority system enforces strict role based access control that immediately blocks unauthorized intent execution pairs, evaluates lineage and scope integrity through a composite risk metric that weights resource consumption, authorization chain depth, and cryptographic verification against a configurable threshold, and guarantees audit completeness by requiring every submitted action to possess a correspondingtrace record before execution can proceed. The network constraints domain tracks topologystability by measuring the relative Frobenius norm change rate of the adjacency matrix across discrete time steps, while the safety and containment domain mandates isolation enforcement by quarantining compromised actors through zero degree graph isolation, and the semantic and large language model domain computes a projection residual that measures the embedding distance between an action semantic vector and a trust weighted centroid, ensuring alignment with policy constrained latent space. When an action is submitted, the fabric evaluates all fourteen primitives concurrently and routes the decision through one of three deterministic pathways. If any hard constraint registers a positive violation value, the system immediately rejects the action, restores the prior system state from a snapshot buffer, and logs the rejection with full diagnostic metadata. If only soft constraints are violated, the action is passed to the projection engine, which formulates a convex quadratic optimization problem that minimizes the Euclidean distance between the original and projected resource cost vectors while enforcing explicit upper bounds and unit normalization constraints. The optimizer executes using the sequential least squares programming method, and upon successful convergence, returns an adjusted action that preserves the original operational intent while satisfying all soft boundary conditions. If the optimization fails to converge, the system defaults to the original cost vector and logs a warning, maintaining operational continuity without compromising safety. This projection mechanism is the defining feature of the fabric, transforming constraint enforcement from a punitive gatekeeper into an adaptive corrective layer that maximizes system utility while guaranteeing boundary compliance. The fabric long term stability is maintained by an adaptive feedback controller that continuously tunes the sensitivity weights of each primitive through a proportional integral architecture with explicit anti windup protection. The controller computes a violation error signal by comparing the observed binary violation status against a configurable target rate, typically set to ten percent, and applies proportional and integral gains to generate a gradient that adjusts the corresponding theta parameter. The integral term is strictly bounded to prevent parameter explosion during sustained violation periods, and all theta values are constrained within a stable range between zero point three and three point zero to ensure numerical robustness.Over the course of the fifty step validation simulation, the controller successfully converged the adaptive parameters, lowering sensitivity for frequently violated hard constraints like resource envelope, trust drift, Byzantine score, authority validity, and audit completeness to the minimum bound of zero point three, while allowing softer monitoring primitives like topology stability and projection residual to relax toward one point zero, demonstrating the system capacity to dynamically recalibrate its enforcement posture in response to observed environmental conditions. Every evaluation cycle, regardless of outcome, is permanently recorded in a cryptographic audit chain that guarantees tamper evident provenance and deterministic replay capability. Each log entry contains a complete diagnostic snapshot including the actor identity, operational intent, resource target, unique identifier, confidence score, decision classification, current state vector, causal counter array, raw and normalized violation scores for all fourteen primitives, and the full projection optimization log. The entry is serialized using strict deterministic formatting with sorted keys and fixed separators, then hashed using SHA-256 alongside the previous entry hash to form an immutable linked chain. The audit structure employs a bounded memory duque to prevent resource exhaustion, and includes a verification routine that recomputes the entire hash chain from genesis to confirm structural integrity. In the validation run, all fifty entries were successfully verified with zero hash mismatches, producing a final chain hash that cryptographically seals the entire execution sequence and enables third party forensic auditing without requiring trust in the underlying system state. The fifty step simulation produced a highly deterministic distribution of outcomes that validates the fabric design philosophy. Zero actions were executed without modification, confirming the system baseline posture of continuous constraint evaluation. Twenty four actions, representing forty eight percent of the total, were successfully adjusted by the projection engine to satisfy soft boundary conditions, demonstrating the optimizer efficacy in preserving operational utility under constraint pressure. Twenty six actions, or fifty two percent, were rejected due to hard constraint violations, with authority validity accounting for twenty eight percent of all rejections, audit completeness failures responsible for eighteen percent, temporal expirations and causal ordering delays each contributing six percent, and the remaining rejections distributed across composite authority and network stability thresholds.Primitive violation statistics revealed that trust drift and projection residual registered one hundred percent violation rates by design, functioning as continuous monitoring signals rather than binary gates, while state consistency, resource envelope, state transition feasibility, belief divergence, Byzantine score, and isolation enforcement maintained zero violation rates, indicating accurate baseline calibration. The adaptive controller successfully constrained all theta parameters within the target stability window, with topology stability exhibiting the highest final sensitivity at approximately zero point nine five, while the core enforcement primitives stabilized at the lower bound. Stress testing across four distinct degradation scenarios confirmed the system predictable failure characteristics and graceful degradation pathways. Under normal operating conditions, the fabric produced nine adjusted actions and one rejection, maintaining balanced constraint enforcement. During simulated trust collapse, where all trust vectors were forcibly reduced tonear zero values, the system adapted by increasing reliance on structural and authority constraints, yielding eight adjustments and two rejections. Network partition scenarios, which zeroed the adjacency matrix to simulate complete communication breakdown, triggered topology stability violations and isolation protocols, resulting in seven adjustments and three rejections as the system prioritized

title: Integrating Corpus Linguistics and NLP Methods to Explore Social Media Discourse from Edinburgh and London
abstract: Abstract The availability of social media data and tools to (semi-)automatically analyse them has sparked research in various fields to assess human behaviour, opinions and attitudes on a global scale. Besides challenges with data preprocessing to ensure the quality of the database, improving the accuracy of automated classifications, such as topic modelling and sentiment analysis, is frequently discussed in natural language processing (NLP) and beyond. In discourse studies, the interpretability of automated classifications is important for integrating such tools into more fine-grained textual analyses. For instance, the distinction into positive and negative polarity rendered by sentiment analysis constitutes a starting point for assessing human perceptions and opinions, but the mere polarity labels do not necessarily allow for interpreting the meaning of sentiments across topics. To explore this, we use Twitter data from Edinburgh and London posted during the COVID-19 pandemic and assess emerging topics and their evaluation. Focussing on methodological aspects, we integrate corpus-linguistic methods to validate and complement NLP techniques to study urban discourses. This study thus contributes to enhancing the toolkit for corpus-assisted discourse analysis, and, at the same time, underscores the value of linguistic insights for social sciences research.
